scenes.heading: ReAct: Reason + Act
scenes.narration: Let's explore ReAct, the pattern that interleaves thinking and doing so an agent's plan becomes explicit and steerable.

scenes.heading: Thought, Action, Observation
items: Thought: the model reasons in plain language
Action: the model names a tool and its input
Observation: your code fills in the tool's result
scenes.narration: ReAct structures every step as three labeled parts. A Thought, where the model reasons out loud about what to do next. An Action, where it names a tool and the input to run. And an Observation, which your code fills in with the tool's actual result. The model writes Thought and Action; you execute and supply the Observation. That repeating triple is the entire pattern.

scenes.heading: Why interleaving wins
steps: You run the tool and return the Observation
The Observation reshapes the next Thought
Stop generation at 'Observation:' so it can't fake it
Repeat until the model emits a finish action
scenes.narration: The power is that reasoning and acting feed each other. The Thought chooses the next Action, you run the tool and hand back the Observation, and that evidence reshapes the following Thought. Critically, you must stop generation at the word Observation, or the model will hallucinate its own tool result. You keep cycling until it emits a finish action. That beats planning everything up front, which can't react to what tools return.

scenes.heading: Parsing the trace
scenes.narration: Because ReAct is just a text convention, your code has to parse it. This regex pulls the tool name and its input out of the Action line. If nothing matches, we bail. Otherwise we look the tool up in our dictionary, run it with the parsed argument, and the result becomes the next Observation we feed back. That unglamorous parsing is the half that turns a free-text trace into a real control loop.

scenes.text: Native tool-calling is today's default; when you hand-roll ReAct, guard against rambling and repetition loops.
scenes.narration: One last thing: modern models offer native tool-calling that returns a structured call, so it's the reliable default and skips fragile parsing. Hand-rolled ReAct still shines when you want a visible reasoning trace or lack a tool API. Either way, guard against its two classic failures, rambling Thoughts and repetition loops, with tight prompts, a step cap, and no-progress detection.
